newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica money mkt rates jump, shortage above 9 bln.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica money mkt rates jump, shortage above 9 bln.

text.p: South African short-term rates jumped again on Monday as the money market shortage continued above nine billion rand and foreigners shunned rand assets, keeping a tight vice on liquidity.
Money market traders said pressure on liquidity would continue until around the end of January as Christmas spending was likely to exacerbate the situation.
Three-month NCD rates jumped to between 16.90 to 17.10 percent from 16.75 to 16.90 percent on Friday, while the 90-day BA rate was at 16.25 to 16.45 from 16.10 to 16.25 percent.
The Reserve Bank indicated the daily shortage above nine billion again on Saturday at 9.191 billion rand from 9.189 billion on Friday.
Dealers said the upcoming Christmas period would see a big notes and coin outflow, ruling out any significant easing in pressures.
"With the shortage as high as it is at the moment, people are negative and sentiment is turning around," one dealer said.
"Notes and coins, which start flowing out of here by the middle of November, only come back in the second or third week of January and that has a major effect on the shortage."
Another trader said "There's just no money available."

Money market rates are now more than discounting a one-percent hike in the Bank rate, currently at 16 percent, but dealers were uncertain whether Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals would bow to the market pressure just yet.
Nedcor senior economist Kevin Lings said a there is a strong case for an official rate hike, but Reserve Bank Governor Chris Stals was holding back.
"There's a whole combination of factors which make a fairly convincing argument that an increase in interest rates is necessary," Lings said.

"But the Reserve Bank has to be careful about increasing rates at a time when we want to increase economic growth and increase investment...high interest rates generally discourage fixed investment," he said.
"The balance is that we don't expect the Reserve Bank to increase interest rates for the moment."
The bank would monitor the situation very closely over the next couple of weeks for signs of continued tightening of liquidity, he said.
